Alright, Friday. You made it. Grab a coffee, let's get you up to speed before you pretend to work.

**Money Talk**

- **AI stocks on a rollercoaster after midterms.**
  First, investors panicked after the Democrats' midterm sweep, fearing new regulations would hamstring AI development and wiping trillions off tech valuations. Now, after a quick collective breath, those same stocks are climbing back, because apparently, President Trump's AI build-out push isn't slowing down, blue wave or not. Classic market jitters. [S6][S7][S12][S15]

- **Fed Chair hints at more rate hikes to tame inflation.**
  San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly dropped a not-so-subtle hint that "higher rates are likely to be needed" to fight inflation. While she called the latest jobs report "good news," it seems the Fed isn't done tightening the screws on your wallet. [S3]

- **Microsoft shifts its AI cloud strategy, less Oracle, more self-reliance.**
  Looks like Microsoft is getting serious about its own AI infrastructure, reportedly winding down its deal with Oracle for AI cloud capacity and focusing on its own data centers. Maybe they got tired of sharing the sandbox, or it’s a cost-saving play given the massive AI buildout costs. [S4][S37]

- **Food banks getting cooked by rising costs.**
  In a grim sign of the times, a food bank in Goole, UK, is set to close in January. Rising operational costs and dwindling donations are hitting the front lines, even as local authorities scramble with "winter support" plans. Someone's getting left in the cold. [S8][S9]

- **UK government demands salary transparency.**
  The UK Prime Minister is telling firms to publish salaries in job adverts ahead of a new law. The pitch is that it'll help jobseekers and fight pay discrimination. My take? Might just make everyone realize how underpaid they are. [S10]

**World Lore**

- **Europe's skies hit by another wave of coordinated bomb threats.**
  Just when you thought it was safe to fly, a fresh flurry of bomb threats disrupted flights across Europe today, affecting at least 18 planes and some media organizations. Luckily, all affected aircraft landed safely and nothing was found – but this coordinated chaos is a real pain in the logistics. [S11][S22]

- **Iran turns up the heat in the Strait of Hormuz, tanker attacked.**
  Iran is apparently back to its old tricks, with a Greek-owned tanker hit by a missile and two other vessels reportedly on fire in the Persian Gulf. One seafarer was killed. If this escalates, expect your Amazon Prime delivery to get a lot more expensive. [S33]

- **Data center protests erupt in Amsterdam, go global.**
  Activists broke into a Microsoft data center in Amsterdam, demanding a pause on new construction. They're organizing protests in 16 countries, arguing the AI building boom is a massive drain on water and power grids, threatening climate goals. Fair point, those server farms ain't running on good vibes. [S35]

- **Kenyan cult leader gets 200 years for child murders.**
  Paul Mackenzie, the leader of a Kenyan doomsday cult, was sentenced to a staggering 200 years in prison. He was convicted of murdering 190 children and one adult after ordering his followers to starve themselves to death to "meet Jesus." Truly chilling stuff. [S23]

- **Thomas Markle arrested in US on child sex abuse material charges.**
  Well, this is a bombshell. Meghan Markle's estranged father, Thomas Markle, was arrested by US federal agents in Florida on child sex abuse material charges. Duchess Meghan is reportedly "deeply distressed." Talk about family drama reaching a new low. [S32]

**Tech Tea**

- **AI-powered cyber warfare gets scarier, faster.**
  Forget slow, manual hacks. State-backed actors are now leveraging AI to launch cyberattacks with "remarkable speed and scale," hitting everything from crypto exchanges (Binance lost $6 billion in a scam linked to fake job interviews) to national espionage campaigns. Also, Chinese AI models are apparently getting frighteningly good at hacking. Your fridge could be next. [S2][S18][S53]

- **Meta's Muse AI launches "Spaces" for customized app experiences.**
  Meta's AI assistant, Muse, is evolving with "Spaces," allowing users to create custom, app-like experiences within the AI itself—think a shopping hub, school dashboard, or a trivia game. It’s like an app store within an AI, which is either brilliant or terrifyingly self-referential. [S42][S47]

- **Tesla officially kills the Cybertruck production.**
  In news that surprises absolutely no one who's seen the thing, Tesla is winding down production of the Cybertruck. Its "bulk and crude shape" apparently couldn't pass regulatory standards outside of "more permissive markets." RIP, you glorious, unloved, utterly absurd polygonal pickup. [S34][S55]

- **White House IP addresses reportedly available for rent for "a few dollars."**
  You heard that right. Security researchers found that software on the presidential network *could* allow outsiders to rent access to White House IP addresses for chump change. If true, that's not just a security hole; it's a security canyon. [S49]

- **Kobo launches subscription for syncing your own ebooks.**
  Amazon's main e-reader competitor, Kobo, is rolling out a new monthly subscription service called Stack. It lets you upload and sync your personal ebooks and documents across your devices, complete with reading progress and annotations. Finally, a way to pay a monthly fee for *your own books*. [S50]

**Creator Szn**

- **Amazon's shopping agent now takes text orders, complete with ads.**
  Your new personal shopper from Amazon is now accepting text message orders. The kicker? The entire thread where you place those orders will be peppered with Sponsored Product ads. Because nothing says seamless consumer experience like an AI trying to upsell you mid-chat. [S56]

- **Instagram chases long-form creators, but is it enough?**
  Instagram is making a big play for long-form video creators, hoping to poach them from YouTube. The question is, can they offer enough exposure and monetization to make it worth the jump? YouTube money talks, Instagram still feels like it's figuring out its voice. [S57]

- **Holiday marketing still belongs to celebrities, not creators.**
  Despite leaning on creators for most of the year, marketers are still defaulting to traditional celebrities for the crucial holiday crunch. Guess when it comes to peak shopping season, brands prefer the predictable, big-name endorsement over authentic creator influence. [S59]

**Supply Lines**

- **Zipline valuation soars past $21B, expands Walmart drone delivery.**
  Drone delivery startup Zipline is absolutely flying, topping a $21 billion valuation after raising new funds and dramatically expanding its partnership with Walmart to 300 new drone sites. This is a massive leap for last-mile autonomy, pushing drone delivery into serious mainstream logistics territory. [S94][S95]

- **Amazon to hike and "streamline" shipping fees in 2027, adds Uber Eats perks.**
  Get ready for more changes from the e-commerce giant: Amazon plans to increase and streamline its shipping and logistics fees starting in 2027. Meanwhile, Prime members just scored $0 delivery fees with Uber Eats, replacing their Grubhub perk. It's a classic Amazon move: give a little, take a little (more). [S90][S91][S92][S93]

- **FedEx amps up holiday logistics with AI, robotics, and new Asia-US flights.**
  FedEx is getting smart for peak season, rolling out AI-enabled tools, robotics, and predictive tech to optimize holiday deliveries. They're also adding five weekly Asia-U.S. cargo flights, signaling confidence in trans-Pacific demand. Plus, they just landed a deal with the US Army to modernize depot logistics. [S85][S87][S88]

- **DHL Group reports Q3 revenue increase, raises annual outlook.**
  DHL is looking strong, reporting a revenue increase in the third quarter of 2026 and bumping up its annual search outlook. This, even as the broader air cargo market sees fortunes divided, with access to freighter capacity proving a key differentiator. [S72][S83]

- **Aurora's autonomous truck production hit by supply and quality issues.**
  Autonomous trucking company Aurora is facing delays in its truck production schedule, citing supply and quality problems with its upfitting partner, Roush. While they still expect over 1,000 trucks by late 2027, it highlights the challenges of scaling advanced tech in heavy industry. [S66]

- **Container spot rates calm, but Middle East tensions loom for ocean freight.**
  After some recent volatility, container spot rates are seeing a bit of calm, with slight declines on key transpacific and Asia-Europe routes as capacity eased. However, the "fragile" Middle East, especially with renewed Strait of Hormuz attacks, remains a significant threat to stability and insurance costs. [S71]

- **Fleetworthy launches AI-powered fleet management tech for smarter ops.**
  Logistics tech startup Fleetworthy just launched RADAR, a new AI-driven platform designed to help fleet managers monitor spending, identify toll discrepancies, and make operational decisions without drowning in reports. Less manual drudgery, more intelligent insights—exactly what the industry needs. [S63]

**Speed Round**

- The Pentagon is dropping $250M on a battery startup, because who needs oil when you have microwaves?
- San Francisco Fed Prez thinks your household finances are feeling the squeeze, no kidding.
- Fox finally snagged Roku for $22 billion – streamers, prepare for more Murdoch.
- Perth logistics startup Indrus just banked $750k in pre-Seed funding, keep an eye on them.
- A former UPS site in Pennsylvania is getting eyed for a massive warehouse project.
- Voters told politicians "Don't B.S. us" in the midterms. Good luck with that.
- A judge just halted construction on Trump's arch, moments after it got federal approval.
